titre: Gresham Never Stated the Law That Bears His Name
accroche: Copernicus describes the mechanism as early as 1517, two years before the birth of Thomas Gresham, to whom the law would nonetheless be attributed three centuries later.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the mid-16th century, England goes through what historians call the Great Debasement: to finance his wars, Henry VIII has coins struck in which pure silver is gradually diluted with copper, a practice continued under his son Edward VI. The old coins, still full of silver, don't disappear from the strongboxes: they disappear from circulation: everyone keeps them, melts them, or exports them, and spends only the debased coins, whose face value officially remains the same. When Elizabeth I takes the throne, in 1558, the financier Thomas Gresham, the Crown's agent in Antwerp, urges the new queen to restore sound money: advice she will follow in the years that follow.

## A Pole had already written it, forty years earlier

What Gresham observes in London, a Polish astronomer and canon had nonetheless already formulated elsewhere, with no known link between the two men. Nicolaus Copernicus, tasked by the King of Poland Sigismund I with advising Royal Prussia on the crisis of its currency, sets down on paper as early as 1517 a first memorandum, *De aestimatione monetae*, which he reworks in 1519 at Olsztyn. He presents it to the Prussian Diet meeting at Grudziądz in 1522, before drawing from it, in 1526, the definitive Latin treatise, *Monetae cudendae ratio*, submitted to the diet of 1528. Copernicus lays out there the same mechanism that Gresham would observe in London a generation later: when a debased coin circulates at equal face value with a coin of good quality, it is the bad one that stays in circulation, because everyone hoards or exports the good one.

## The name that stuck isn't the author's

Nothing in Thomas Gresham's surviving writings states the principle in the general form attributed to him today: he advises a specific monetary policy, he doesn't state a general law. It is the British economist Henry Dunning Macleod who, in 1857, decides to christen the phenomenon “Gresham's law,” nearly three centuries after the events, thereby choosing an English name and an English episode over the Polish memorandum that predates it by forty years, or the even earlier examples that historians find in classical antiquity, the Near East, and China. The mechanism remains correct: it is its address that is wrong. A law still bears today the name of the financier who applied it, not of the astronomer who demonstrated it first.

repere.texte: Copernicus writes his first memorandum on debased currency in 1517, two years before Thomas Gresham was even born (c. 1519). It is the economist Henry Dunning Macleod who, in 1857, chooses to name the phenomenon after Gresham rather than after Copernicus.

carte.punch: Gresham's law was written by a Pole, forty years before Gresham.
carte.idee: Nicolaus Copernicus describes as early as 1517 the mechanism by which bad money drives good money out of circulation, two years before Thomas Gresham was even born. Yet it is Gresham's name that a Victorian economist chose, in 1857, to christen the phenomenon.

quiz.question: What distinguishes Copernicus's memorandum on money from the law attributed to Gresham?
choix: Copernicus describes the opposite: good money drives out bad
Copernicus never wrote anything about money, only about astronomy
Gresham's law was formulated by Gresham himself, as early as 1558
Copernicus describes the same mechanism, decades before Gresham was associated with its name
quiz.explication: Copernicus writes his memorandum on debased currency as early as 1517, before Gresham was even born; it is the economist Henry Dunning Macleod who, in 1857, chooses to name the phenomenon after Gresham rather than after Copernicus, who had described it first.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who gives Gresham's law its name, and when?
choix: Henry Dunning Macleod, a British economist
Nicolaus Copernicus, who had formulated it first
Thomas Gresham, who stated it himself
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1857, the British economist Henry Dunning Macleod christens the phenomenon “Gresham's law,” nearly three centuries after the events, rather than after Copernicus, who had described it as early as 1517.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why do pure silver coins disappear from circulation in England in the mid-16th century?
choix: Because they are banned by a royal decree
Because they are all melted down to finance Henry VIII's wars
Because everyone keeps them, melts them, or exports them rather than spending them
Because the Crown officially withdraws them from the market in 1558
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Debased coins and coins full of silver circulate at the same face value; everyone hoards, melts, or exports the good money and spends only the bad, whose value remains unchanged on paper.
